semantics.note: Keeps the 'as far as I can tell' qualifier and both parts (no real data, no hypothetical label). That qualifier marks the limits of his knowledge; it does not put a probability on the outcome, so this stays an observation.

contract.note: Judging the graph and how it was presented, not Marcus's private knowledge, is a fair, ordinary reading. The support and contradiction conditions are balanced, but both need the original graph to be identified.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps both halves and the repeated 'by all accounts', which claims broad agreement. Adds nothing and drops nothing.

contract.note: The result depends on reading 'by all accounts' as broad agreement and on using o1-preview against GPT-4o. That reading is ordinary. Comparing with GPT-4o, a later and stronger GPT-4 model, if anything helps Marcus.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own evaluation reports o1-preview preferred by a large margin in data analysis, coding and math. It is a company disclosure, so it weighs less, but it is still a contemporary account of large gains.
An independent test before the post: o1-preview scored near-perfect on a math exam that GPT-4o scored well below. It shows a substantial gain, though only in one domain.
METR's independent tests found limits in autonomous agent tasks, but also strong reasoning and better one-step code generation. Mixed qualifying context.
Compares GPT-4 with GPT-3.5, not GPT-3, so it does not directly settle the first half.

reviews.rationale: The claim says everyone agreed the GPT-4-to-o1 gain was modest. Contemporary accounts before the post, including an independent math evaluation and OpenAI's own multi-domain results, describe large reasoning gains. METR's limits qualify this but do not restore universal agreement. The first half is not independently settled, but the joint claim fails on its second half.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words. He is the one making the Altman 'AGI' remark an example; the remark itself is not the claim.

semantics.note: 'Lots of hype' softens 'bullshit' but keeps the meaning. The first half is an evaluative remark; the checkable core is that none of the Rubik's cube robotics promises shipped.

contract.note: Focusing on the robotics claim and treating 'shipped' as externally available is ordinary and fair. The result depends on identifying what was actually promised, which Marcus did not specify.

evidence.note: The original 2019 OpenAI campaign post. It states an ambition toward general-purpose robots but names no product or delivery, so it neither confirms nor disproves a broken promise.
A May 2024 report that OpenAI revived its robotics team. It shows no shipped product, but it is not a full release record.

reviews.rationale: The packet does not establish any specific promised deliverable, or a complete release record through October 2024. The campaign shows only a stated ambition. The general remark about marketing has no measure. The evidence is insufficient either way.

attribution.note: Marcus's own analogy in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Rather than delivered results' adds a contrast Marcus did not state; he said only 'to a large extent' based on promise. Saying what drove a valuation is a causal claim, as the contract's axis already treats it, not a plain observation.

contract.note: The contract reads 'to a large extent' as substantial but not exclusive and makes no fraud claim. That is fair. But nothing tells us how much of the valuation came from promise, so the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: Reuters, Oct 2024: investors were anticipating growth based on Altman's projections, but the piece also cites real revenue and user growth. Partial and unmeasured, so context only.
OpenAI's funding announcement stresses current adoption. A company disclosure; it does not show how investors weighed adoption against expectations.

reviews.rationale: The evidence shows that growth expectations mattered to investors and that real adoption also existed. Nothing separates how much of the valuation came from each, and there is no representative sample of press coverage. Neither condition is met.
